items.title: IoC & Dependency Injection
items.context: Inversion of Control (IoC) means the Spring container — not your code — creates and wires objects (beans). Dependency Injection (DI) is how IoC is implemented: dependencies are supplied to an object rather than the object creating them itself, via constructor, setter, or field injection.

questions.prompt: What does Inversion of Control mean in Spring?
choices: Your code manually creates and wires every object it needs
All beans must be stateless
The Spring container controls object creation and wiring instead of your application code
Spring reverses the order methods are called in
questions.explanation: IoC flips who's in charge: instead of your code instantiating and wiring dependencies itself, the Spring container does it and hands beans to you.

questions.prompt: Which form of dependency injection is generally recommended for required dependencies?
choices: XML-only injection
Setter injection
Field injection with @Autowired
Constructor injection
questions.explanation: Constructor injection makes required dependencies explicit and immutable, and makes the class easy to unit test without a Spring container — the generally preferred approach for mandatory dependencies.

items.title: Stereotype annotations
items.context: @Component is the generic Spring-managed bean annotation. @Repository marks a DAO and adds exception translation. @Service marks business-logic beans. @Controller marks a web MVC controller, and @RestController combines @Controller with @ResponseBody for building REST APIs.

questions.prompt: Which stereotype annotation additionally provides automatic exception translation for data-access code?
choices: @Repository
@Service
@Component
@Controller
questions.explanation: @Repository is specialized for the DAO layer and translates persistence-technology exceptions into Spring's unified DataAccessException hierarchy.

questions.prompt: What does @RestController combine?
choices: @Repository and @Transactional
@Configuration and @Bean
@Controller and @ResponseBody
@Component and @Service
questions.explanation: @RestController = @Controller + @ResponseBody, so every handler method's return value is serialized straight into the HTTP response body (typically as JSON).

items.title: Bean lifecycle
items.context: A bean's lifecycle: instantiation, dependency injection, any Aware callbacks, then @PostConstruct / InitializingBean.afterPropertiesSet(), then it's ready for use, and finally @PreDestroy / DisposableBean.destroy() on shutdown.

questions.prompt: In what order do these happen for a Spring bean: (a) dependency injection, (b) constructor call, (c) @PostConstruct method?
choices: a, b, c
c, b, a
b, c, a
b, a, c
questions.explanation: Spring first constructs the bean (b), then injects its dependencies (a), and only then invokes any @PostConstruct-annotated initialization method (c).

questions.prompt: Which annotation marks a method to run just before a singleton bean is destroyed?
choices: @Scope
@PostConstruct
@PreDestroy
@Bean
questions.explanation: @PreDestroy-annotated methods run during container shutdown, right before the bean is discarded — commonly used to release resources like connections.

items.title: Bean scopes
items.context: Common Spring bean scopes: singleton (one shared instance per container — the default), prototype (a new instance every time it's requested), plus web-aware scopes like request and session.

questions.prompt: What is the default scope of a Spring bean if none is specified?
choices: session
prototype
singleton
request
questions.explanation: Unless you annotate otherwise (e.g. @Scope("prototype")), Spring manages exactly one shared instance of a bean per container — that's the singleton scope.

items.title: Aspect-Oriented Programming
items.context: AOP modularizes cross-cutting concerns (logging, security, transactions) into aspects instead of scattering them through business code. A Pointcut defines *where* an aspect applies (which join points); Advice defines *what* runs there (before/after/around).

questions.prompt: In Spring AOP, what does a Pointcut define?
choices: The code to execute when advice runs
The transaction isolation level
The bean's scope
An expression matching which join points the advice should apply to
questions.explanation: A Pointcut is the 'where' — an expression selecting which methods/join points an aspect's advice should be woven into.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a classic example of a cross-cutting concern handled well by AOP?
choices: A single class's private helper method
Business validation logic unique to one method
Logging applied consistently across many unrelated methods
A DTO's getters and setters
questions.explanation: Logging (like security and transaction management) tends to be needed across many unrelated methods/classes — exactly the kind of concern AOP lets you modularize instead of duplicating everywhere.

items.title: Java configuration classes
items.context: Instead of (or alongside) component scanning, Spring beans can be declared explicitly in a @Configuration class, where each @Bean-annotated method returns an object Spring registers and manages.

questions.prompt: Which annotation marks a class as a source of bean definitions written in plain Java?
choices: @Component
@Repository
@Value
@Configuration
questions.explanation: @Configuration marks a class whose @Bean methods Spring calls to obtain and register bean instances — an explicit, code-based alternative to relying purely on component scanning.

items.title: ApplicationContext vs BeanFactory
items.context: BeanFactory is the basic Spring IoC container, providing core dependency-injection capabilities. ApplicationContext extends BeanFactory with extra features: event publication, internationalization, and easier integration with AOP and declarative transaction management.

questions.prompt: What does ApplicationContext add on top of the basic BeanFactory?
choices: The ability to define beans at all
Support for only XML configuration
Nothing, they're identical
Additional enterprise features like event propagation and easier AOP/transaction integration
questions.explanation: ApplicationContext is a superset of BeanFactory's core DI functionality, adding event handling, message-source support, and smoother integration with Spring's AOP and transaction infrastructure — which is why almost every Spring application uses an ApplicationContext rather than a bare BeanFactory.

items.title: Circular dependencies
items.context: A circular dependency (bean A needs bean B, which needs bean A) can be resolved by switching from constructor injection to setter/field injection for one side, or by marking one dependency @Lazy so its initialization is deferred until first use.

questions.prompt: Beans A and B each require the other via constructor injection, causing a circular dependency error at startup. What's a common fix?
choices: Rename the classes
Increase the application's heap size
Switch one side to setter injection, or mark one dependency @Lazy
Give up on dependency injection entirely for these beans
questions.explanation: Constructor injection requires both beans fully built before either can be constructed, which a genuine cycle makes impossible. Setter injection or @Lazy breaks the cycle by deferring when one dependency is actually needed.

items.title: @Value & externalized configuration
items.context: @Value injects a single configuration value — from application.properties/application.yml, an environment variable, or a literal — directly into a field, constructor parameter, or setter.

questions.prompt: Which annotation injects a single property value (e.g. from application.properties) into a field?
choices: @Value
@Autowired
@Bean
@Component
questions.explanation: @Value("${some.property}") pulls a single externalized configuration value into a field, constructor parameter, or setter argument.

items.title: @Qualifier for disambiguating beans
items.context: When more than one bean matches the type Spring is trying to autowire, injection becomes ambiguous unless you disambiguate — typically with @Qualifier("beanName") to pick a specific one, or @Primary to mark a default.

questions.prompt: Two beans both implement PaymentGateway, and a class autowires a PaymentGateway field. What happens without further guidance?
choices: Spring throws a NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException unless disambiguated (e.g. with @Qualifier or @Primary)
The application falls back to no injection at all
Both beans are injected into the same field automatically
Spring picks one at random silently
questions.explanation: Autowiring by type fails with an ambiguity exception when multiple candidates match; @Qualifier names the specific bean to inject, and @Primary marks one candidate as the default choice.

items.title: Profiles
items.context: @Profile("name") restricts a bean to only be registered when that profile is active — a common way to swap configuration (e.g. a real payment gateway vs a fake one) between dev, test, and production environments.

questions.prompt: What does @Profile("dev") on a bean definition do?
choices: Registers that bean only when the "dev" profile is active
Makes the bean a singleton
Disables the bean entirely
Runs the bean only on Mondays
questions.explanation: @Profile restricts a bean's registration to environments where the named profile is active, letting you swap implementations (e.g. mock vs real services) per environment.

questions.prompt: How is a Spring profile typically activated?
choices: By renaming the jar file
Via the spring.profiles.active property (config file, env var, or command-line argument)
Profiles cannot be changed once compiled
Automatically based on the OS
questions.explanation: Setting spring.profiles.active=dev (in application.properties, an environment variable, or a JVM argument) tells Spring which profile-scoped beans to activate at startup.

items.title: Component scanning
items.context: @ComponentScan tells Spring which package(s) to scan for classes annotated with @Component (and its specializations like @Service/@Repository/@Controller), registering matches as beans automatically. Spring Boot's @SpringBootApplication includes it implicitly, scanning from the main application's package downward.

questions.prompt: What does @ComponentScan control?
choices: Which beans get destroyed first on shutdown
Which HTTP methods a controller accepts
The database connection pool size
Which package(s) Spring scans for annotated components to register as beans
questions.explanation: @ComponentScan tells Spring where to look for classes carrying stereotype annotations (@Component, @Service, @Repository, @Controller) so it can register them as beans without manual XML/Java configuration for each one.

items.title: @Lazy initialization
items.context: By default, singleton beans are created eagerly at container startup. @Lazy defers a bean's creation until it's first actually needed, which can speed up startup or break certain circular-dependency situations — at the cost of pushing any construction errors to first-use time instead of startup.

questions.prompt: What does @Lazy on a bean definition change?
choices: The bean is created on a background thread
The bean can no longer be autowired
The bean becomes prototype-scoped
The bean isn't created until it's first actually requested, instead of at container startup
questions.explanation: @Lazy defers instantiation from container startup to the point of first use — useful for expensive beans that aren't always needed, or to sidestep certain circular-dependency issues.

items.title: BeanPostProcessor
items.context: A BeanPostProcessor hooks into the container's bean-creation pipeline, running custom logic before and/or after every bean's initialization callbacks — the extension point behind many Spring features (like processing @Autowired or @Async annotations).

questions.prompt: What is a BeanPostProcessor used for?
choices: Only for beans explicitly marked @PostProcess
Logging HTTP requests
Running custom logic before/after the initialization of every bean in the container
Replacing the need for a bean's constructor
questions.explanation: BeanPostProcessor implementations are applied to every bean the container creates, letting Spring (or your own code) inspect, wrap, or modify beans right around their initialization step — much of Spring's 'magic' annotation processing is built this way.

items.title: Environment abstraction
items.context: Spring's Environment abstraction provides a single, unified way to read properties regardless of where they came from — application.properties, environment variables, system properties, or command-line arguments — and to know which profiles are currently active.

questions.prompt: Which Spring abstraction provides unified access to configuration properties from multiple sources (files, env vars, system properties, ...)?
choices: Environment
PropertyFile
ApplicationContext
BeanFactory
questions.explanation: Environment merges multiple underlying PropertySources into one consistent API (getProperty(...)) and also exposes which profiles are currently active, so code doesn't need to know or care exactly where a value came from.

items.title: Autowiring by type vs by name
items.context: Spring's default autowiring strategy is by type — it looks for a bean matching the required type. When multiple beans of that type exist, it falls back to matching by field/parameter name before giving up and requiring @Qualifier or @Primary to disambiguate.

questions.prompt: What is Spring's default autowiring strategy when injecting a dependency by type?
choices: By type — Spring looks for a bean assignable to the required type
Autowiring never happens without explicit configuration
By bean name only, ignoring type
Randomly among all beans
questions.explanation: @Autowired resolves by type first; only when several candidates of that type exist does Spring try matching by the field/parameter name, and ultimately may require @Qualifier or @Primary to pick one unambiguously.

items.title: @Import and modular configuration
items.context: @Import on a @Configuration class pulls in one or more additional @Configuration classes, letting you compose configuration from smaller, focused modules instead of one monolithic class.

questions.prompt: What does @Import(OtherConfig.class) on a @Configuration class do?
choices: Marks OtherConfig as deprecated
Deletes OtherConfig's beans
Includes OtherConfig's bean definitions as part of this configuration, letting you compose configuration from multiple classes
Imports a Java package for use in code
questions.explanation: @Import lets one @Configuration class pull in another's bean definitions, supporting a modular style where configuration is split across focused classes and assembled together where needed.

items.title: Prototype beans injected into singletons
items.context: If a singleton bean simply @Autowired-injects a prototype-scoped dependency as a normal field, it only ever gets ONE instance of that prototype — created once, when the singleton itself is built — defeating the point of prototype scope. Fixing this requires a scoped proxy, an ObjectFactory/Provider, or looking the bean up from the context on each use.

questions.prompt: A singleton service @Autowires a prototype-scoped dependency directly as a field. What's the problem with this setup?
choices: The application fails to start
There is no problem — a fresh prototype instance is created on every method call
Prototype beans cannot be autowired at all
The singleton only ever receives one instance of the prototype, created once at startup, since the field is only injected once
questions.explanation: A plain @Autowired field is resolved once, when the singleton is constructed — so despite being 'prototype' scoped, only a single instance ever gets injected. Getting a fresh prototype per use requires a scoped proxy, or injecting an ObjectFactory<T>/Provider<T> and calling get() each time.

items.title: Spring application events
items.context: Spring beans can publish custom events via ApplicationEventPublisher.publishEvent(...) and other beans can react to them with an @EventListener method — a decoupled way for parts of an application to communicate without directly calling each other.

questions.prompt: How does one Spring bean typically notify other, unrelated beans that something happened, without calling them directly?
choices: Restarting the ApplicationContext
Publishing an event via ApplicationEventPublisher, consumed elsewhere by an @EventListener method
Throwing an exception and letting the caller catch it
Using a static shared variable
questions.explanation: Publishing through ApplicationEventPublisher and reacting via @EventListener decouples the publisher from any specific listener — the publisher doesn't need to know who (if anyone) is listening.

items.title: Stereotype meta-annotations
items.context: @Service, @Repository, and @Controller are themselves annotated with @Component (they're meta-annotated) — which is exactly why component-scanning, which looks for @Component, picks them up too.

questions.prompt: Is @Service itself annotated with @Component?
choices: Yes — @Service is meta-annotated with @Component, which is why component-scanning detects @Service-annotated classes too
Only when used together with @Autowired
Only in Spring Boot, not plain Spring
No, they are completely unrelated annotations
questions.explanation: @Service (like @Repository and @Controller) carries @Component as a meta-annotation on its own declaration, so anything that looks for @Component during component-scanning finds @Service-annotated classes as well.

items.title: @PostConstruct vs constructor logic
items.context: Initialization logic that depends on injected dependencies should go in an @PostConstruct method, not the constructor — at construction time, field/setter injection hasn't necessarily run yet, so dependencies may still be null.

questions.prompt: Why put dependency-dependent initialization logic in an @PostConstruct method instead of directly in the constructor?
choices: At construction time, field/setter-injected dependencies may not be set yet; @PostConstruct is guaranteed to run only after all injection is complete
@PostConstruct runs faster than constructor code
Constructors cannot contain any logic in Java
It's purely a style preference with no functional difference
questions.explanation: With field or setter injection, dependencies are set after the object is constructed — so relying on them inside the constructor risks NullPointerExceptions. @PostConstruct is explicitly guaranteed to run only once dependency injection has fully completed.

questions.prompt: Which interface's afterPropertiesSet() method is the older, interface-based equivalent of an @PostConstruct method?
choices: InitializingBean
ApplicationContextAware
BeanFactoryAware
DisposableBean
questions.explanation: InitializingBean.afterPropertiesSet() predates @PostConstruct as a way to run initialization logic once a bean's properties have been set, though the annotation-based approach is more common in modern code.

items.title: Aware interfaces
items.context: Implementing an *Aware interface (like BeanNameAware or ApplicationContextAware) lets a bean be automatically handed access to a piece of Spring's own infrastructure — its own bean name, or a reference to the ApplicationContext itself — that it wouldn't otherwise have any way to obtain.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of implementing ApplicationContextAware on a bean?
choices: It prevents the bean from being autowired
It marks the bean as a singleton
It gives the bean a callback (setApplicationContext) through which Spring hands it a reference to the ApplicationContext itself
It's required for every Spring bean
questions.explanation: *Aware interfaces are Spring's mechanism for injecting framework infrastructure objects (the bean's own name, the ApplicationContext, the BeanFactory, ...) into a bean that needs direct access to them, via a setter callback Spring calls automatically during initialization.

items.title: Conditional bean registration
items.context: @ConditionalOnProperty (and the more general @Conditional) let a bean be registered only if some condition holds at startup — commonly a property being set to a particular value — enabling optional features that can be toggled through configuration without code changes.

questions.prompt: What does @ConditionalOnProperty(name = "feature.x.enabled", havingValue = "true") on a bean do?
choices: Registers that bean only if the property feature.x.enabled is set to "true" at startup
Always registers the bean regardless of configuration
Deletes the property if the bean fails to load
Nothing unless combined with @Component
questions.explanation: Conditional annotations let bean registration itself depend on runtime configuration — this specific one only creates the bean when the named property matches the expected value, a common way to build optional/toggleable features.

items.title: FactoryBean
items.context: A FactoryBean<T> is itself a Spring bean, but its job is to produce a different object (of type T) via its getObject() method — used when constructing the real bean needs custom logic too complex for a constructor or simple @Bean method (e.g. building a complex third-party client object).

questions.prompt: What is a FactoryBean in Spring?
choices: A synonym for @Component
A bean that can never be autowired
A special bean whose getObject() method produces the actual bean instance that gets registered and injected elsewhere
A bean that creates other Spring configuration classes
questions.explanation: Rather than being injected directly, a FactoryBean is a container-recognized indirection: Spring calls its getObject() to obtain the actual bean instance, which is what gets registered under that bean name and injected wherever it's needed — useful for complex construction logic.

items.title: ObjectProvider for optional or repeated lookups
items.context: Injecting an ObjectProvider<T> (or javax/jakarta Provider<T>) instead of a plain T lets a bean gracefully handle a dependency that might not exist, or repeatedly obtain a fresh instance on demand — notably solving the 'prototype bean injected into a singleton' problem by calling getObject() each time a fresh instance is needed.

questions.prompt: How does injecting an ObjectProvider<T> instead of a plain T help when a singleton needs a fresh prototype-scoped instance on each use?
choices: Calling objectProvider.getObject() each time triggers a fresh lookup, giving a new prototype instance per call instead of one fixed instance from construction time
ObjectProvider converts the prototype into a singleton
It requires XML configuration to work
It doesn't help; ObjectProvider behaves exactly like a direct injection
questions.explanation: Unlike a directly-injected field (resolved once, at construction), each call to ObjectProvider.getObject() asks the container for the bean again — for a prototype-scoped dependency, that means a genuinely fresh instance every time, solving the classic singleton-holding-a-prototype problem.

items.title: SpEL in @Value
items.context: @Value can hold a Spring Expression Language (SpEL) expression, not just a plain ${property} placeholder — enabling defaults (${prop:default}), arithmetic, and even referencing other beans' properties directly in the annotation.

questions.prompt: What does @Value("#{2 * 5}") inject into a field?
choices: The integer 10, since #{...} evaluates a SpEL expression
null
A compile error, since @Value only accepts property placeholders
The literal string "2 * 5"
questions.explanation: #{...} in @Value triggers SpEL evaluation rather than a simple ${...} property lookup — here it evaluates the arithmetic expression 2 * 5 and injects the resulting value, 10.

items.title: Property source precedence
items.context: When the same property is defined in multiple places, Spring resolves it using a defined precedence order — command-line arguments and environment variables generally take priority over values in application.properties/application.yml, letting deployment-time overrides win without editing packaged config files.

questions.prompt: If a property is defined both in application.properties and as a command-line argument (--some.prop=value) at startup, which one generally wins?
choices: application.properties always wins
The command-line argument, since command-line args sit higher in Spring's property source precedence
Whichever was loaded first, non-deterministically
Neither — Spring throws an error on conflicting values
questions.explanation: Spring's Environment abstraction resolves properties through an ordered list of PropertySources; command-line arguments and environment variables sit above the packaged application.properties/yml, letting you override configuration at deploy/run time without touching the built artifact.

items.title: @Qualifier overrides @Primary
items.context: When both are present, an explicit @Qualifier at the injection point wins over a bean marked @Primary — @Primary just sets the default tiebreaker, while @Qualifier is a specific instruction for that one injection point.

questions.prompt: If bean B is marked @Primary but an injection point specifies @Qualifier("A") for a different bean A of the same type, which bean gets injected?
choices: Neither — this always throws an error
Bean A — an explicit @Qualifier at the injection point takes precedence over the general @Primary default
Both are injected into a List automatically
Bean B, since @Primary always wins
questions.explanation: @Primary establishes a fallback default when nothing more specific is stated; @Qualifier is an explicit, targeted instruction for one particular injection point, and explicit beats default.

items.title: Overriding a bean definition
items.context: If two bean definitions are registered under the same name, by default the later one registered overrides the earlier one (Spring Boot disables this 'bean overriding' by default since 2.1, throwing an error instead, unless explicitly re-enabled).

questions.prompt: In modern Spring Boot (2.1+) with default settings, what happens if two different configuration classes each define a bean with the same name?
choices: Both beans coexist as separate instances
Startup fails with an error, since bean-definition overriding is disabled by default
The second definition silently overrides the first, as in older Spring versions
Spring picks one at random
questions.explanation: Spring Boot 2.1 flipped the default to disallow bean overriding, since silent overrides were a common source of confusing bugs — attempting to redefine the same bean name now fails fast at startup unless you explicitly opt back in.

items.title: Abstract bean definitions
items.context: A bean definition can be marked abstract, serving only as a configuration "template" that other concrete bean definitions inherit shared settings from (e.g. common properties) — the abstract definition itself is never instantiated.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of marking a bean definition as abstract in Spring's XML/Java configuration?
choices: It hides the bean from autowiring only
It marks the bean as thread-unsafe
It creates a reusable configuration template that other concrete bean definitions can inherit shared settings from, without being instantiated itself
It's required for every interface-typed bean
questions.explanation: An abstract bean definition exists purely to be a parent template — child bean definitions inherit its configured properties/settings, reducing duplication, while the abstract one is never itself instantiated as a real bean.

items.title: Constructor vs setter injection trade-offs
items.context: The common guidance: use constructor injection for mandatory, required dependencies (guarantees the object can never exist in an incomplete state) and setter injection for optional dependencies that may reasonably be absent or changed after construction.

questions.prompt: What is the general guideline for choosing between constructor and setter injection?
choices: Constructor injection for mandatory/required dependencies; setter injection for optional ones
Always use setter injection for everything
Constructor injection is deprecated in favor of setter injection
It makes no difference which you choose
questions.explanation: Constructor injection makes a dependency non-optional and guarantees the bean is never in a half-constructed state without it; setter injection is better suited to genuinely optional dependencies that might not always be supplied or might change later.

items.title: @Transactional self-invocation

questions.prompt: Does saveOrder() actually run inside a transaction here?
choices: Only if placeOrder() is also annotated @Transactional
It throws an exception at startup
Yes — @Transactional always applies regardless of how the method is called
No — calling saveOrder() from within the same class (self-invocation) bypasses Spring's proxy, so no transaction is started
questions.explanation: @Transactional (like most Spring AOP features) works by wrapping the bean in a proxy that intercepts calls made *through it from outside*. Calling saveOrder() as `this.saveOrder()` from inside placeOrder() never goes through that proxy — it's a plain Java method call — so the transactional advice never fires. The usual fixes are moving saveOrder() to another bean, or injecting the bean into itself to force calls through the proxy.

items.title: Circular dependency via constructor injection

questions.prompt: What happens when Spring tries to start this application context?
choices: Only bean A fails to start; B starts fine
Starts fine — Spring resolves the cycle automatically
Compile error
Throws BeanCurrentlyInCreationException describing a circular dependency
questions.explanation: Constructor injection requires a bean's full dependency to exist before construction — A needs a B to be constructed, but B needs an A, and neither can finish first. Spring detects this circular chain and fails fast at startup with BeanCurrentlyInCreationException, rather than silently guessing. Field or setter injection can resolve this specific case because Spring can create the raw instances first and inject afterward — but a circular *constructor* dependency is a hard error by design.

items.title: Ambiguous @Autowired candidates

questions.prompt: What happens when Spring tries to wire UserService?
choices: Throws NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException — two beans match the JpaRepository<User, Long> type
Picks the first matching bean alphabetically
Starts fine; repo is left null
Wires both beans into a List automatically
questions.explanation: @Autowired by type fails when more than one bean satisfies that type and there's no @Primary or @Qualifier to disambiguate — Spring throws NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException listing the candidates. The fix is adding @Qualifier("userRepository") at the injection point, or marking one repository @Primary.

items.title: Prototype bean injected into a singleton

questions.prompt: How many distinct Task instances does Scheduler ever see?
choices: Exactly one — the prototype Task is injected once, when the singleton Scheduler is created, and reused forever after
It depends on how many HTTP requests are handled
Spring throws an exception mixing scopes like this
A new Task on every method call, as expected from a prototype bean
questions.explanation: Plain field/constructor injection resolves the dependency once, at the moment the singleton Scheduler bean is constructed — after that, Scheduler just holds a reference to that one Task instance forever, defeating the purpose of the prototype scope. Getting a fresh Task per use requires an injected ObjectFactory<Task>/Provider<Task>, a lookup-method, or a scoped proxy — this mismatch between an outer singleton and an inner prototype is one of the most common Spring scoping mistakes.

items.title: Exception in @PostConstruct

questions.prompt: What happens when the Spring application context starts?
choices: init() runs lazily on first use instead
The exception is logged and swallowed
The whole ApplicationContext fails to start — Spring wraps the exception in a BeanCreationException
Startup fails to start, but the rest of the context starts fine
questions.explanation: @PostConstruct runs as part of bean initialization, which happens eagerly during context startup for singleton beans by default. An exception there isn't isolated to that one bean — it propagates up and Spring wraps it in a BeanCreationException, which aborts starting the entire application context. This is why a single misconfigured bean can take an entire Spring Boot app down at boot.

items.title: Missing @Value placeholder with no default

questions.prompt: What happens when Spring tries to create this bean?
choices: Spring silently skips this field
limit is left uninitialized (Java default)
Startup fails: the placeholder "${feature.limit}" can't be resolved
limit is set to 0
questions.explanation: Spring's property placeholder resolution fails fast: if a ${...} placeholder has no matching property and no default value syntax (${feature.limit:100}), context startup throws an exception (typically wrapping IllegalArgumentException: "Could not resolve placeholder"). It won't silently leave the field at 0 — that would hide a real configuration mistake.

items.title: Mutable state on a singleton bean

questions.prompt: What is the risk with this bean as written?
choices: Spring throws an exception because singleton beans can't have mutable fields
count is shared, mutable state on a singleton bean — concurrent requests can race and produce incorrect results
None — Spring gives each request its own Counter instance
count resets to 0 on every request automatically
questions.explanation: By default, a @Service is a singleton — exactly one instance serves every request, concurrently, on whatever threads the container hands it. A plain, unsynchronized int field mutated by ++count is exactly the shared-state race condition problem: two threads can interleave their read-increment-write and lose an update, same as any other unsynchronized shared counter. Singleton beans should generally be stateless, or use thread-safe state (AtomicInteger) if they must hold counters.

items.title: Circular dependency via field injection

questions.prompt: Does this circular dependency start successfully, unlike the constructor-injection version?
choices: It depends on bean creation order, and is unreliable
Yes — Spring can construct the raw A and B instances first (no-arg constructors), then inject the fields afterward, breaking the cycle
Yes, but only one of the two beans actually gets its field set
No — field injection has the exact same restriction as constructor injection
questions.explanation: Field and setter injection don't require the dependency to be present at construction time — Spring can instantiate A and B with their default constructors first, register them as "currently being created", and then wire the @Autowired fields into each other afterward. This is exactly why constructor injection (recommended for immutability) surfaces circular dependencies as hard startup failures, while field injection can silently paper over the same design smell.

items.title: @Bean methods calling each other in @Configuration

questions.prompt: How many Engine instances does the context actually create — one shared by both Car and Truck, or two independent ones?
choices: Two — engine() is called twice in plain Java, once from car() and once from truck()
It throws a BeanCreationException for calling a @Bean method directly
It depends on the declaration order of car() and truck()
One — Spring CGLIB-proxies the @Configuration class so calling engine() again returns the same cached singleton bean instead of re-running the method
questions.explanation: In "full" @Configuration classes (the default), Spring generates a CGLIB subclass of AppConfig at startup. Calls to another @Bean method from within the class are intercepted by that proxy: instead of actually re-running engine()'s body, it checks the container for an existing 'engine' singleton and returns that. So both car() and truck() end up sharing the exact same Engine instance, honoring Spring's default singleton scope even though the Java source looks like two ordinary method calls.

items.title: @Autowired with zero matching beans

questions.prompt: What happens when Spring tries to start this application context?
choices: Throws NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException
Throws NoSuchBeanDefinitionException — no bean of type PaymentGateway exists to satisfy the dependency
Spring creates a default no-op implementation automatically
Starts fine; gateway is left null until first used
questions.explanation: @Autowired fields are required by default. If zero beans match the requested type anywhere in the context, Spring fails fast at startup with NoSuchBeanDefinitionException, rather than leaving the field null and letting it blow up later as an NPE. This is the mirror image of NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException (too many matches) — here there are too few. Making the dependency optional requires @Autowired(required = false) or an Optional<PaymentGateway> injection point.
